title: Lion Head Meatballs
subtitle: Large braised pork meatballs nestled in soft napa cabbage
excerpt: Lion head meatballs are a celebrated dish from Jiangsu province: large, loosely packed pork balls made with water chestnuts for texture, braised slowly in stock with napa cabbage until the leaves are silky and the meatballs are deeply flavoured and tender. Serves 4 in about 75 minutes.
sourceNotes: Lion head meatballs, known in Chinese as shi zi tou, are a classic of Huaiyang cuisine from the Jiangsu-Anhui region, one of the four great culinary traditions of Chinese cooking. The dish is discussed in Yan-Kit So's 'Classic Food of China' (Macmillan, 1992) and in Fuchsia Dunlop's 'Land of Fish and Rice' (Bloomsbury, 2016), which covers Jiangnan cooking and traces the dish's name to the resemblance between the large meatball surrounded by ruffled cabbage and the head of a lion with its mane.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked meatballs without the cabbage in their braising liquid for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight and reheat gently on the hob, adding fresh blanched cabbage to finish.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The meatballs can be shaped and refrigerated uncooked for up to 24 hours. The whole dish reheats very well the next day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A classic dish of Jiangsu cuisine in which large pork meatballs, roughly the size of a fist, are braised slowly with napa cabbage in a light stock. The name refers to the visual resemblance of the meatball, surrounded by ruffled cabbage leaves, to a lion's head with its mane. The meatballs are deliberately loosely packed to stay tender, unlike the dense, bouncy meatballs used in other Chinese dishes.

Also called Chinese leaf or Chinese cabbage, napa cabbage has pale, tightly packed, crinkled leaves with broad white ribs. It is more delicate in flavour than round green cabbage and becomes silky and sweet when braised. It is widely used in Chinese, Korean and Japanese cooking.

The corm of an aquatic plant, used extensively in Chinese cooking for their crisp texture, which they retain even after cooking. In meatballs they add a pleasant crunch and lightness. Tinned water chestnuts are widely available and work well here; drain and rinse before use.

A Chinese fermented rice wine named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. It has a rich, slightly nutty flavour and is used in marinades, braises and sauces throughout Chinese cooking. Dry sherry makes a reasonable substitute.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 75 minutes in total.
Lion head meatballs
are larger than a tennis ball, loosely packed, and braised rather than fried, which is what makes them so tender. Each meatball feeds one person as a main course with rice.
The
water chestnuts

are not optional: they add lightness and a little crunch that breaks up the richness of the pork. Use a fatty mince, at least 20% fat, or the meatballs will be dense. Handle the mixture as little as possible when shaping, just enough to hold together. The
napa cabbage
goes in for the last 20 minutes and becomes deeply tender, absorbing the braising liquid.
What you need
Method

Combine the {{pork-mince}}, {{water-chestnuts}}, {{ginger}}, {{spring-onions}}, {{shaoxing-wine}}, {{soy-sauce}}, {{sesame-oil}}, {{cornflour}}, egg, sugar and white pepper in a bowl. Stir in one direction for 1 to 2 minutes until the mixture holds together and feels slightly springy. Do not overwork it.
Divide the mixture into 4 equal portions, about 200g each. With wet hands, gently shape each into a rough ball. Do not compact them tightly.

Heat the {{vegetable-oil}} in a wide, deep pot or wok over a medium-high heat. Gently lower the meatballs in and brown lightly on all sides, about 4 to 5 minutes total. They will be fragile at this stage, so turn carefully.
Pour in the {{chicken-stock}}, remaining soy sauce and
shaoxing wine
. Bring to a simmer. Cover and cook over a low heat for 30 minutes.
Tuck the {{napa-cabbage}} pieces around and under the meatballs. Replace the lid and braise for a further 20 minutes until the cabbage is completely soft and the meatballs are cooked through.
Taste the broth and adjust the seasoning. Serve the meatballs and cabbage in deep bowls with the broth ladled over and steamed rice on the side.

items.symptom: The meatballs are falling apart during browning
items.cause: The mixture was not mixed enough or the meatballs were compacted too loosely
items.fix: Make sure the mixture feels cohesive before shaping. Wet your hands well before forming each ball and handle them gently. A pair of large spoons can help to lower them into the pan.

items.symptom: The meatballs are dense and rubbery
items.cause: The mixture was overworked or the pork was too lean
items.fix: Stop mixing as soon as the ingredients are combined. Use pork with at least 20% fat content.

items.symptom: The broth is thin and watery
items.cause: Not enough soy sauce or the stock was weak
items.fix: Add another tablespoon of soy sauce and check the seasoning. A small splash of dark soy sauce can be added for colour and depth without much extra salt.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Lion head meatballs are a classic dish of Jiangsu province, one of the Eight Great Cuisines of China. The braised version is a winter dish. A steamed summer version also exists. The large meatball surrounded by cabbage leaves is said to look like a lion with its mane, which gives the dish its name.
